Clinical Reference

Hypertensive Emergency

On this page
Severe hypertension (usually >180/120 mmHg) with acute, ongoing hypertension-mediated organ damage — brain, eyes, heart, aorta, kidneys, or placenta. The organ damage, not the number, defines the emergency: it needs a titratable IV agent in a monitored bed, not a rapid "normalization."
BP usually >180/120 Rule = ↓MAP ≤25% in hour 1 Target-organ damage = the discriminator First-line drips: nicardipine · clevidipine · labetalol Aortic dissection: SBP <120 & HR <60 in 20 min
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Arterioles normally autoregulate: when perfusion pressure rises they constrict to keep tissue blood flow constant, and when it falls they dilate. In a hypertensive crisis, blood pressure rises so far or so fast that this myogenic reflex is overwhelmed. The vessel wall is subjected to mechanical shear and stretch beyond its capacity → endothelial injury → loss of nitric-oxide–mediated vasodilation, platelet and fibrin deposition, and leak of plasma proteins into the vessel wall (fibrinoid necrosis, the histologic hallmark of malignant hypertension). The damaged endothelium releases vasoconstrictors and activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). Angiotensin II raises pressure further and is directly toxic to the endothelium, closing a vicious cycle: pressure → injury → RAAS → more pressure. Meanwhile pressure natriuresis dumps salt and water, so many patients are paradoxically volume-depleted — a reason a reflexive diuretic or aggressive drop can trigger organ hypoperfusion.

The end-organs fail wherever this plays out. In the brain, breakthrough of cerebral autoregulation causes hyperperfusion, capillary leak and vasogenic edema → hypertensive encephalopathy / PRES. In the eye, the same fibrinoid necrosis produces flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilledema (grade III–IV retinopathy). In the kidney, arteriolar injury drives acute kidney injury and a thrombotic microangiopathy. In the heart/aorta, the pressure load causes acute LV failure/flash pulmonary edema, demand ischemia, or propagation of an aortic dissection.

Think of arterioles as garden hoses with a pressure-relief valve (autoregulation). Crank the spigot slowly and the valve keeps the spray steady. Crank it wide open, fast, and the valve is overwhelmed — the hose wall balloons, splits, and leaks. And because the brain has spent weeks resetting its own valve to the higher pressure, if you now slam the spigot shut too fast, the brain — used to high pressure — is suddenly starved. That is why the rule is "lower firmly but gradually," not "normalize."

Pressure overwhelms autoregulation → endothelial injury/fibrinoid necrosis → a self-amplifying RAAS loop → end-organ failure. The organ column is the "hypertension-mediated organ damage" that upgrades severe hypertension to an emergency.
In chronic hypertension the whole autoregulation plateau shifts right: the brain now depends on a higher MAP for adequate flow, and its lower limit has risen from ~60 to ~90–110 mmHg. Drop MAP more than ~25% and you fall off the left edge into cerebral ischemia — the mechanistic basis of the "≤25% in the first hour" rule.
Grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy: flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and AV nicking — the fundus is the one place you directly see the small-vessel injury.
Frank Wood, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Renal arteriolar hyalinosis (H&E): pink, glassy protein deposited in the arteriolar wall — the chronic counterpart of the acute fibrinoid necrosis that drives hypertensive AKI.
Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0 — Wikimedia Commons
Every drug in this guide targets one step of that cascade. Dihydropyridine CCBs (nicardipine, clevidipine) block L-type Ca²⁺ channels → arteriolar smooth-muscle relaxation (attacks the raised systemic vascular resistance directly). β-blockers (labetalol, esmolol) cut heart rate and aortic wall shear (dP/dt) — the reason they lead in dissection. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside) donate NO to replace what the injured endothelium can't make (venodilation unloads the congested heart). Phentolamine blocks α-receptors for catecholamine excess. ACE-inhibitors (enalaprilat) and fenoldopam interrupt RAAS / add dopaminergic renal vasodilation. Match the lesion to the lever.
🗂️

Classification — the fork that decides everything

The single most important triage step is separating a true emergency from severe hypertension without organ damage. They look identical on the monitor and are managed completely differently.

CategoryBPAcute organ damage?Where & how to treat
Hypertensive emergencyUsually >180/120 (can be lower, e.g. eclampsia, acute pulmonary edema)YES — brain/eye/heart/aorta/kidney/placentaICU/monitored bed, IV titratable agent, arterial line for most
Asymptomatic severe HTN (formerly "urgency")>180/120NODo NOT lower acutely in the ED. Restart/intensify oral meds, arrange close outpatient follow-up (days). Rapid IV lowering causes harm.
Malignant / accelerated HTNUsually >180/120 (often diastolic >120–130)YES — grade III–IV retinopathy ± AKI/TMAA subtype of emergency; treat as emergency with IV therapy
The term "hypertensive urgency" is being retired — the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline and ACEP frame the no-organ-damage patient as asymptomatic severe hypertension precisely because "urgency" wrongly implies you must lower the pressure urgently. You must not.
🎯

BP targets by syndrome — the one table to memorize

"How fast and how low" depends entirely on which organ is failing. This table is the operational core of the guide; the drips and cautions in the ICU tab flow from it.

SyndromeTarget & speedFirst-line agent(s)Avoid / caution
General emergency (encephalopathy, AKI, malignant HTN)↓MAP ≤25% in hour 1 → ~160/100–110 over 2–6 h → normal over 24–48 hNicardipine or clevidipineDo not "normalize" fast — cerebral/renal/coronary hypoperfusion
Aortic dissectionSBP <120 AND HR <60 within ~20 minβ-blocker FIRST (esmolol/labetalol) → then add nicardipine/nitroprussideNever vasodilate before rate control (reflex tachycardia ↑ aortic shear)
Acute ischemic stroke — tPA/thrombectomy candidate<185/110 before lytic, then <180/105 × 24 hLabetalol or nicardipine—
Acute ischemic stroke — no reperfusionPermissive: treat only if >220/120 (↓~15% in 24 h)Labetalol or nicardipineLowering BP can extend the infarct (penumbra)
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)Presenting SBP 150–220: lower smoothly to SBP 130–140 (INTERACT3 bundle, target <140)Nicardipine or clevidipineDon't overshoot <130 or drop >60 mmHg in 1 h (ATACH-2 harm); avoid nitroprusside (↑ICP)
Acute pulmonary edema / LV failureRapid afterload/preload reductionNitroglycerin (± nitroprusside) + loop diureticAvoid β-blockers acutely (negative inotropy); avoid pure vasoconstrictors
ACS / myocardial ischemiaRelieve ischemia; ↓ demandNitroglycerin + β-blockerAvoid hydralazine (reflex tachycardia); no NTG if RV infarct / recent PDE5-inhibitor
Sympathetic crisis (cocaine, amphetamine, pheo, MAOI)Control adrenergic surgePhentolamine, benzodiazepines, nicardipine/nitroprussideNO unopposed β-blockade → unopposed α vasoconstriction/crisis
Pre-eclampsia with severe features / eclampsiaTreat sustained ≥160/110 → target <160/<110 (keep DBP ~85–105)IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or PO/IV nicardipine + magnesium (seizure ppx)Avoid ACEi/ARB (fetal toxicity); nitroprusside only as last resort (fetal cyanide)
Two numbers are life-or-death outliers from the "gradual ≤25%" rule: aortic dissection wants SBP <120 fast, and ischemic stroke without reperfusion wants you to mostly leave the pressure alone (permissive to 220/120). Everything else is "firm but gradual."
🩺

Presentation — symptoms/signs, frequency & why

Presentation is organ-specific: the same pressure declares itself through whichever bed is failing. Frequencies below are approximate, drawn from emergency-department hypertensive-crisis registries (STAT/Studying the Treatment of Acute hyperTension and ED series).

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens
Headache~40–55%Cerebral hyperperfusion/vasogenic edema stretching pain-sensitive dura and vessels; classic in encephalopathy/PRES.
Chest pain~25–30%Demand ischemia (↑afterload/wall stress), ACS, or aortic dissection — always the "can't-miss" triad to sort out.
Dyspnea~25–30%Acute diastolic dysfunction + afterload mismatch → flash pulmonary edema; high LA pressure floods alveoli.
Neuro deficit / altered mentation~20–25%Ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke, or global encephalopathy from breakthrough hyperperfusion and cerebral edema.
Visual disturbance / blurring~15–20%Retinal hemorrhage/exudate, papilledema, or occipital PRES edema (cortical visual symptoms).
Grade III–IV retinopathy on fundoscopy~15–20%Fibrinoid necrosis of retinal arterioles → flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilledema = malignant HTN.
Nausea / vomiting~10–15%Raised ICP from cerebral edema, or a feature of encephalopathy/PRES.
Epistaxis~10%Rupture of fragile nasal (Kiesselbach) vessels under high pressure.
Focal back/tearing pain, pulse deficit<10%Aortic dissection — the highest-stakes presentation; interarm BP difference, widened mediastinum.
Seizure<10%Cerebral edema (encephalopathy/PRES) or eclampsia; a neurologic emergency within the emergency.
Oliguria / rising creatinine, hematuria<10% overtAcute hypertensive nephrosclerosis / thrombotic microangiopathy injuring glomeruli.
Read the patternA patient with a very high BP and no acute symptoms or signs is asymptomatic severe HTN, not an emergency — the workup below is precisely how you prove or exclude organ damage before you decide to reach for a drip.
🪛

StudyOrder whenKey finding & meaning
12-lead ECGEvery patientLVH with strain (chronic load), ischemia/STEMI (a precipitant or consequence), arrhythmia.

Non-contrast CT: acute intracerebral hemorrhage. Hypertensive bleeds classically sit in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons or cerebellum — the deep perforator territory.

🧪

Reading the labs — why each value moves

LabWhat it tells you & why it moves
Creatinine / BUNRises with acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis and thrombotic microangiopathy. A new bump = active renal target-organ damage (an emergency); a stable chronic elevation is not. Over-rapid BP lowering can also drop GFR (renal hypoperfusion).
UrinalysisHematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts signal glomerular/vascular injury — bedside evidence the kidney is being hit right now.
TroponinElevated from demand ischemia (↑wall stress) or true ACS. A rising trend points to myocardial injury as cause or consequence.
BNP / NT-proBNPUp with acute LV wall stress in flash pulmonary edema; supports a cardiac cause of the dyspnea.
CBC + smear (LDH, haptoglobin, schistocytes)Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, thrombocytopenia) = malignant HTN thrombotic microangiopathy; overlaps with TTP/HUS and HELLP — check when creatinine/BP are severe.
ElectrolytesPressure natriuresis + secondary hyperaldosteronism → hypokalemia; screen for primary aldosteronism (secondary-HTN workup) when unexplained low K⁺.
Urine tox / metanephrinesCocaine/amphetamine (sympathetic crisis) or pheochromocytoma; changes the drug (phentolamine, no unopposed β-block).
Pregnancy test (β-hCG), LFTs, uric acidAny woman of childbearing age — identifies pre-eclampsia/HELLP, which has its own drugs (labetalol/hydralazine/nicardipine + magnesium) and forbids ACEi/ARB.
Left ventricular hypertrophy — the chronic pressure-overload adaptation. On ECG it produces high voltages with strain; it also stiffens the LV, priming the diastolic failure behind flash pulmonary edema.
Patrick J. Lynch, medical illustrator, CC BY 2.5 — Wikimedia Commons
Confirm the reading: correct cuff size, arm at heart level, repeat in both arms. An interarm SBP difference >20 mmHg is itself a dissection clue; a spuriously high reading can manufacture a false "emergency."
Jacek Halicki, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons
🩺 Clinic — the severe reading in front of you, and chronic control
Assess

A very high BP in clinic — is it an emergency?

🔍

Triage the number vs the organ

Most markedly elevated office readings are asymptomatic severe hypertension, not emergencies. Your job is a focused screen for acute organ damage. If it's absent, you do not lower the pressure acutely — you fix the chronic regimen and follow up.

First, confirm the reading: correct cuff size, arm supported at heart level, patient rested 5 min, repeat after a few minutes and in both arms. A large interarm difference (>20 mmHg SBP) is itself a clue to dissection/peripheral disease.

Ask the "organ" questions on the spot: chest pain, dyspnea/orthopnea, focal weakness/speech change, severe headache, visual change, confusion, pregnancy. Any "yes" → treat as possible emergency and send to the ED, don't titrate an oral pill.
ScreenLooking for
HistoryChest/back pain, dyspnea, neuro deficit, headache, visual change, pregnancy, cocaine/stimulant use, medication non-adherence.
ExamFocal neuro signs, papilledema/retinal hemorrhage on fundoscopy, pulmonary crackles, new murmur, pulse/BP asymmetry.
Point-of-careECG (ischemia/LVH), urinalysis (proteinuria/hematuria), creatinine — only if symptoms or per judgment (ACEP: not mandatory if truly asymptomatic).

Do-not-harm

Asymptomatic severe HTN — what NOT to do

🛑

The number is scary; the reflex is wrong

A patient at 210/120 who feels well, has a normal exam, and no acute organ-damage evidence has asymptomatic severe hypertension. The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline explicitly advises against using IV or oral agents solely to acutely lower BP here — rapid drops cause more harm (stroke, MI, syncope) than the transient high number.

  • Do: restart or up-titrate the patient's oral regimen; identify why BP rose (non-adherence, NSAIDs, salt, stimulants); arrange follow-up within days to ~1 week.
  • Don't: give sublingual/immediate-release nifedipine, IV boluses, or "treat to a number" in the office/ED.
Sublingual/immediate-release nifedipine is never appropriate for a BP number — its abrupt, uncontrolled drop has caused stroke, MI and death (long-standing AAFP/ACEP safety warning).
Treat

Chronic control — first-line → escalation

💊

Stepwise oral therapy (goal <130/80, 2025 AHA/ACC)

Preventing the next crisis is a chronic-control problem. Thiazide-type diuretics deplete volume, CCBs relax arterioles, and ACEi/ARBs interrupt RAAS — the same three levers you pull acutely, in slow-release form.
1
First-line — pick one (or start two if BP >20/10 above goal)
Thiazide-type diuretic, DHP-CCB, or ACEi/ARB are co-equal first-line.
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Chlorthalidone12.5–25 mg dailydouble q2–4 wk25–50 mg (max 100)Thiazide-like; volume + long-term arteriolar effect. Preferred over HCTZ (better CV-outcome data, longer-acting)HCTZ 12.5–25→50 mg; sulfa concern → CCB/ACEi
Amlodipine5 mg daily↑ to 10 mg after ~6 wkmax 10 mgDHP-CCB — arteriolar vasodilation; excellent in Black patients & isolated systolic HTNPedal edema → reduce dose or switch to ACEi/ARB; nondihydropyridine (diltiazem) if also need rate control
Lisinopril10 mg daily (2.5–5 in CKD/elderly)double q2–4 wkmax 40 mgACEi — blocks angiotensin II; renoprotective in DM/CKD/proteinuriaCough/angioedema → ARB (losartan); pregnancy → contraindicated
Losartan50 mg daily↑ to 100 mgmax 100 mgARB — same RAAS blockade without kinin-mediated cough; mildly uricosuric (good in gout)Do NOT combine with ACEi; pregnancy → contraindicated
2
If above goal — combine (single-pill preferred)
ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide is the standard triple.
▾

Add agents from the other first-line classes rather than maxing one. A logical build is ACEi/ARB + amlodipine → add chlorthalidone. Combining an ACEi/ARB with a CCB reduces the CCB's pedal edema. Never combine an ACEi with an ARB.

3
Resistant HTN (uncontrolled on 3 incl. diuretic)
Add spironolactone; hunt a secondary cause.
▾

Add spironolactone 25 mg daily (the evidence-based 4th agent, PATHWAY-2) — watch K⁺/creatinine. Confirm adherence, remove BP-raising agents (NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants), and complete the secondary-HTN workup (primary aldosteronism, renovascular disease, pheo, OSA). Refer to hypertension specialist/nephrology if still uncontrolled.

Compelling indications override the "any first-line" rule: ACEi/ARB for DM/CKD/proteinuria/HFrEF, β-blocker if there's a separate indication (post-MI, HFrEF, AF rate control) — not first-line for BP alone.

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

AfterRecheck
Starting/uptitrating ACEi/ARB or diureticBMP (K⁺, creatinine) in 2–4 weeks; a <30% creatinine rise on an ACEi/ARB is acceptable.
Any regimen changeBP recheck in 2–4 weeks (home BP log) until at goal, then every 3–6 months.
After an ED visit for asymptomatic severe HTNFollow-up within days to ~1 week; titrate to goal over weeks.
At goal & stableAnnual labs; reinforce lifestyle (DASH diet, sodium <1.5–2.3 g, weight, alcohol, activity).

Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

Red flags → emergency department

Severe BP plus any of: chest or tearing back pain, dyspnea/orthopnea (flash edema), focal neuro deficit or severe headache/confusion, visual loss or papilledema, new AKI or hematuria/proteinuria, pregnancy ≥20 wk with BP ≥160/110 or headache/RUQ pain/visual symptoms. These are hypertensive emergencies — send for IV therapy, do not manage in clinic.
🛏️ Wards — confirmed emergency, IV therapy & the oral transition
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

Any confirmed hypertensive emergency (severe BP + acute organ damage) is admitted — most to an ICU/step-down for continuous BP and organ monitoring with parenteral therapy (2017 ACC/AHA). Severe BP without organ damage generally does not need admission for the pressure alone.

Admit & whereSituation
ICUNeeds continuous IV titratable drip / arterial line: dissection, ICH/SAH, large or reperfused stroke, flash edema on nitrates, ACS with refractory HTN, eclampsia, catecholamine crisis, malignant HTN with TMA/AKI.
Step-down / telemetry floorOrgan damage stabilizing, transitioning off drip to oral, still needs close monitoring.
Observation / dischargeAsymptomatic severe HTN with a reassuring workup — oral meds + rapid follow-up, not an admission for the number.

Calc

MAP & hour-1 target calculator

🧮

Compute MAP and the ≤25% first-hour goal

MAP = (SBP + 2×DBP) ÷ 3. For a general emergency, the first-hour floor is a 25% reduction in MAP — don't go below it in hour 1. This is exact arithmetic (MDCalc "Mean Arterial Pressure").

—
Enter a blood pressure to compute MAP and the first-hour target.
This ≤25% rule is for the general emergency. It does NOT apply to aortic dissection (drive SBP <120 fast) or ischemic stroke without reperfusion (permissive to 220/120) — use the syndrome selector below.

Treat

Acute management

💊

The sequence, on the floor / step-down

1
Confirm emergency & set the target
Organ-damage evidence + which syndrome.
▾

Verify true target-organ damage (don't drip an asymptomatic patient). Establish the syndrome-specific target using the selector above. Place an arterial line for beat-to-beat titration if starting a drip.

2
Start the right IV titratable agent
Nicardipine/clevidipine for most; β-first for dissection; NTG for edema/ACS.
▾

Match the drip to the syndrome (full dose ladders in the ICU tab). Titrate to the target, not to "normal." Reassess q5–15 min.

AgentStartTitrationMaxBest for
Nicardipine5 mg/h↑2.5 mg/h q5–15 min15 mg/hMost emergencies, neuro (no ICP rise)
Clevidipine1–2 mg/hdouble q90 s32 mg/hTight, fast neuro control; avoid egg/soy allergy
Labetalol10–20 mg IV bolusrepeat/double q10 min300 mg (or 0.5–2 mg/min gtt)Stroke, ACS, pregnancy
3
Transition to oral & find the cause
Overlap orals before stopping the drip.
▾

Once organ damage is stabilizing and BP is in the target band, start/resume the oral regimen (see Clinic ladder) and wean the drip with overlap. Address the precipitant (non-adherence, secondary cause, drug/stimulant). Do not discharge on the day the drip stops.

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • BP/MAP — q15 min on a drip (arterial line ideal); confirm you're at the syndrome target, not overshooting.
  • Neuro checks — mental status, focal deficits (encephalopathy/stroke evolution).
  • Renal — creatinine and urine output (both under-diuresis and over-rapid lowering hurt the kidney).
  • Cardiac — serial troponin if ischemia, respiratory status if edema.
  • Electrolytes — K⁺ with diuretics/RAAS agents.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU for: need for a continuous IV titratable infusion or arterial line; confirmed aortic dissection; evolving stroke/ICH needing tight control; refractory pulmonary edema (rising O₂ requirement, NIV/intubation); BP not controlled to target despite escalating boluses; hemodynamic instability; eclampsia (seizure) or pre-eclampsia not responding to first-line IV therapy; malignant HTN with new TMA/AKI.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: organ damage resolving/stabilized; off IV therapy and on an effective oral regimen for ≥24 h with an acceptable BP trajectory; secondary-cause plan in place; and close outpatient follow-up (days to ~1 week) arranged.

Home

BP controlled on orals, no residual deficit, reliable follow-up & adherence support.

Home health

Home + nurse visits for BP checks/med teaching, or new mild deficit needing therapy.

SNF

Post-stroke/ICH needing 24-h skilled nursing but <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Stroke/ICH with functional deficits able to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs (e.g., ventilator weaning after intubation for flash edema).

Hospice / palliative

Devastating hemorrhagic stroke with goals-of-care shift to comfort.
🫀 ICU — titratable drips, beat-to-beat control & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

Which emergencies belong in the unit

Essentially every true hypertensive emergency needs a monitored bed, because they need a continuous IV titratable infusion and beat-to-beat BP control. Those needing an arterial line almost always: aortic dissection, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute ICH/SAH/large ischemic stroke on tight control, acute pulmonary edema on IV nitrates, ACS with refractory HTN, eclampsia, catecholamine/sympathetic crisis, and malignant HTN with TMA/AKI.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Intra-arterial line — beat-to-beat BP for titration; essential for clevidipine/nitroprusside and for dissection (a cuff can't keep pace with the drip).
  • Continuous ECG/telemetry, hourly urine output (renal perfusion), frequent neuro exams.
  • Serial labs — creatinine, troponin, and for nitroprusside >24–48 h or renal/hepatic failure, watch for cyanide/thiocyanate (lactic acidosis, altered mentation).
  • Target the syndrome, not "normal" — set explicit MAP/SBP alarm limits so nursing doesn't overshoot on the low side.

Sodium nitroprussideNO donor → balanced arterial + venous dilation0.25–0.3 mcg/kg/min → ↑0.5 → usual 2–3 → 10 mcg/kg/min (≤10 min at max)seconds / 1–2 minPotent last-resort. Cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity (worse in renal/hepatic failure; co-give thiosulfate); raises ICP (avoid encephalopathy/high ICP); coronary steal in ACS
HydralazineDirect arteriolar dilator10–20 mg IV slow bolus, repeat q4–6 h10–30 min / 2–12 h (erratic)Mainstay in pre-eclampsia. Unpredictable/prolonged → delayed hypotension; reflex tachy (pair with β). Avoid dissection & ACS
EnalaprilatIV ACE inhibitor → blocks angiotensin II1.25 mg IV over 5 min q6 h → up to 5 mg q6 h15–30 min / 12–24 hUnpredictable magnitude. Contraindicated in pregnancy & bilateral renal-artery stenosis; avoid acute MI/high-renin (precipitous drop)
FenoldopamDopamine-1 agonist → renal/splanchnic vasodilation, natriuresis0.1–0.3 mcg/kg/min → ↑0.05–0.1 q15 min → 1.6 mcg/kg/min5–15 min / 30–60 minPreserves renal perfusion → AKI/renal impairment. Reflex tachy; avoid glaucoma (↑IOP); contains sulfites
PhentolamineNonselective α-blocker5 mg IV bolus (1 mg test), repeat; or 0.5–1 mg/min gtt1–2 min / 10–30 minCatecholamine excess (pheo, cocaine, MAOI, clonidine withdrawal). Reflex tachy/flushing
Magnesium sulfateMembrane stabilizer / anticonvulsant (not a primary antihypertensive)4–6 g IV load over 15–20 min → 1–2 g/h infusion— / —Eclampsia seizure ppx/treatment. Monitor reflexes/RR/UOP; antidote calcium gluconate; reduce in renal impairment
Read the table by mechanism: if the problem is high resistance, pick an arterial dilator (nicardipine/clevidipine); if the problem is wall shear/rate (dissection), lead with a β-blocker; if it's a congested heart (edema/ACS), donate NO (nitroglycerin); if it's catecholamines, block α (phentolamine). The syndrome selector in the Wards tab maps each scenario to its agent.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚠️

How the comorbidity changes the drug

SettingPreferAvoid — and why
CKD / AKIFenoldopam (renal perfusion), nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalolNitroprusside (cyanide/thiocyanate accumulation); dose-adjust enalaprilat
Pregnancy / pre-eclampsiaLabetalol, hydralazine, nicardipine/nifedipine; methyldopa (chronic) + magnesiumACEi/ARB & enalaprilat (fetal toxicity); nitroprusside (fetal cyanide); atenolol (IUGR)
Aortic dissectionβ-blocker FIRST (esmolol/labetalol), then nicardipine/nitroprussideAny vasodilator before rate control — reflex tachy ↑ aortic shear & extends the tear; hydralazine
ICH / high ICP / encephalopathyNicardipine, clevidipine, labetalolNitroprusside & nitroglycerin — cerebral vasodilation ↑ ICP; avoid overshoot hypotension
ACS / MINitroglycerin + β-blockerHydralazine (reflex tachy ↑ demand); nitroprusside (coronary steal)
Acute pulmonary edemaNitroglycerin (± nitroprusside) + loop diureticβ-blockers acutely (negative inotropy in decompensated LV); hydralazine
Pheo / cocaine / sympathomimeticPhentolamine + benzodiazepines; nicardipine/nitroprusside/NTGUnopposed β-blockade → unopposed α vasoconstriction → paradoxical crisis
Bilateral renal-artery stenosisCCB, labetalolACEi/ARB (enalaprilat) → acute renal failure
The four never-events: (1) unopposed β-blockade in cocaine/pheo; (2) vasodilator before β-blocker in dissection; (3) nitroprusside with high ICP or renal failure; (4) sublingual nifedipine for any BP number. Each has a documented mechanism of harm.
Airway

Respiratory support (flash edema)

🌬️

NIV first; intubate if it fails

Hypertensive flash pulmonary edema is an afterload-mismatch problem: the fix is nitroglycerin (unload the LV) + NIV, not primarily diuresis (many are euvolemic). Start CPAP/BiPAP early — it reduces preload/afterload and work of breathing and often averts intubation. Intubate for failure to oxygenate/ventilate, exhaustion, or ↓mental status.

Induction/intubation itself causes a catecholamine surge — in dissection or ACS, control BP/HR before laryngoscopy to avoid a pressure spike.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory

⚙️

When first-line drips aren't enough

  • Refractory BP: combine agents by mechanism (arterial dilator + β-blocker); add nitroprusside or fenoldopam; re-hunt a secondary cause (pheo, aldosteronism, renovascular).
  • Aortic dissection type A → emergent cardiothoracic surgery while controlling BP/HR; type B with complications → endovascular repair (TEVAR).
  • Malignant HTN with TMA → BP control usually reverses it; distinguish from TTP/HUS (may need plasma exchange) and HELLP (delivery).
  • Eclampsia → magnesium (load + infusion), delivery is the definitive treatment; control severe-range BP first.
  • Volume: many crisis patients are volume-depleted from pressure natriuresis — cautious fluids can prevent hypoperfusion as BP falls (except in overt pulmonary edema).
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: organ damage is stabilized; the patient has been off IV infusion for ~6–24 h on a stable oral regimen; BP is within the target band without ongoing titration; and there's no active issue (evolving stroke, dissection, refractory edema) needing beat-to-beat control.
Not yet if: still requiring drip up-titration, labile BP with swings, worsening neuro/renal/cardiac markers, or a not-yet-secured aneurysm/undelivered eclampsia. A stable oral regimen with an arranged close follow-up is the real exit criterion — not just a normal number for an hour.
Shared

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The 13 things that change what you do

It's the organ damage, not the number. 230/130 asymptomatic with a normal workup = severe asymptomatic HTN (oral meds, follow-up); 175/95 with a dissection or flash edema = emergency (ICU, IV drip). Treat the syndrome, not the monitor.
≤25% MAP reduction in the first hour for a general emergency, then ~160/100–110 over 2–6 h. Overshoot causes watershed cerebral/coronary/renal infarction because the autoregulation curve is shifted right.
Aortic dissection = rate control BEFORE vasodilation. β-blocker first (esmolol/labetalol) to cut dP/dt; a vasodilator alone provokes reflex tachycardia that increases aortic wall shear and extends the tear. Target SBP <120, HR <60.
Never sublingual/immediate-release nifedipine for a BP number — abrupt uncontrolled drops have caused stroke, MI and death.
Hydralazine is unpredictable and long-acting (erratic 2–12 h response) → delayed hypotension. Avoid in dissection and ACS; pair with a β-blocker for reflex tachycardia.
Nitroprusside = cyanide/thiocyanate risk, worst in renal/hepatic failure and >2 mcg/kg/min; co-give thiosulfate and cap duration. It also raises ICP — avoid in encephalopathy/high ICP.
Never give an unopposed β-blocker in pheochromocytoma or cocaine crisis — unopposed α vasoconstriction can precipitate a hypertensive catastrophe. Use phentolamine (and benzodiazepines for cocaine).
Acute ischemic stroke is permissive — don't treat unless >220/120 (or >185/110 if a tPA/thrombectomy candidate). Lowering BP can extend the infarct (penumbra).
ICH target ~130–140, but don't overshoot below ~130 or drop >60 mmHg in an hour (ATACH-2 harm signal). Use the INTERACT3 care bundle.
Pre-eclampsia: treat severe-range BP (≥160/110) within 30–60 minutes to prevent maternal stroke; give magnesium for seizure prophylaxis (Magpie). Avoid ACEi/ARB and nitroprusside.
Fenoldopam is the friend of the failing kidney — a dopamine-1 agonist that preserves renal blood flow and natriuresis; consider in AKI/renal impairment instead of nitroprusside.
Clevidipine and nicardipine don't raise ICP and titrate smoothly → first-line for neuro emergencies. Clevidipine's lipid vehicle contraindicates it in egg/soy allergy and defective lipid metabolism.
Pulmonary edema hates β-blockers acutely (negative inotropy) — use nitroglycerin + a loop diuretic + NIV instead. And remember many crisis patients are volume-depleted from pressure natriuresis, so cautious fluids may be needed as BP falls.

Refs

Sources, trials & guidelines

🧪

Landmark trials

Trial (year)ResultWhy it matters
SPRINT (2015)Intensive SBP <120 vs <140 → CV events ↓25%, mortality ↓27%; stopped earlyBasis for the chronic <130/80 target (a chronic-control, not emergency, trial).
INTERACT2 (2013)Early SBP <140 in ICH safe; ordinal shift favored intensiveEstablished early intensive lowering is safe and probably beneficial in ICH.
ATACH-2 (2016)SBP 110–139 vs 140–179 → no functional benefit, more renal AEsWarns against overshoot <120; anchors ICH target to ~130–140.
INTERACT3 (2023)Care bundle (early SBP <140 + glucose/fever/reversal) → better 6-mo outcomePractice-changing: bundled early intensive SBP control improves ICH outcomes.
ENCHANTED (2019)Intensive SBP 130–140 vs <180 pre-alteplase → no functional benefit, fewer ICHsSupports <185/110 pre-lytic / <180/105 post-lytic without pushing lower.
RIGHT-2 (2019)Prehospital transdermal GTN vs sham → no benefit despite lower BPDon't routinely/prehospital lower BP in acute stroke.
ECLIPSE (2008)Clevidipine vs NTG/nitroprusside/nicardipine in perioperative HTN → safe, tight controlEvidence base for clevidipine as a precise titratable agent.
SHEP (1991)Chlorthalidone-based tx of isolated systolic HTN → stroke ↓36%Foundational: treating HTN (even ISH) prevents stroke.
Magpie (2002)MgSO₄ vs placebo in pre-eclampsia → eclampsia (seizures) halvedBasis for magnesium seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia.
